AIA.culture: Anguillans live a laid-back island life of fishing, boatbuilding, summer boat races and open-air beach barbecues with reggae and soca music.
AIA.history: Anguilla was settled by Arawak-speaking Taino peoples who left cave art and pottery, and was claimed by England in 1650, becoming a poor, remote British colony with small plantations worked by enslaved Africans. The island stayed so isolated that in 1967 its people rebelled against being governed from distant Saint Kitts, eventually winning a return to direct British rule as a self-governing overseas territory. Today salt ponds and fishing have given way to tourism on some of the Caribbean's most beautiful beaches.
AIA.funFact: Anguilla has no rivers at all, so islanders have always depended on rainwater cisterns and salt ponds.

ATG.culture: Antiguans and Barbudans live for cricket and sailing, celebrate Carnival in late July and August, and eat national dishes like funggee, pepperpot and saltfish.
ATG.history: Antigua was home to Ciboney and Arawak peoples before England settled it in 1632 under Sir Thomas Warner, turning it into a sugarcane colony worked by enslaved Africans, with Nelson's Dockyard at English Harbour as a key British naval base. Slavery ended in 1834 and the islands drifted into a plantation-free economy of tourism and sailing. Antigua and Barbuda became fully independent from Britain on November 1, 1981, keeping a place in the Commonwealth.
ATG.funFact: Antigua claims a beach for every day of the year, 365 in all.

ARG.culture: Argentines share mate tea among friends, dance tango in Buenos Aires, grill enormous asados and treat football almost as a religion.
ARG.history: The land was home to peoples like the Mapuche, Guarani and Inca-influenced Diaguita before Spain colonized it in the 1500s and ruled it through the Viceroyalty of the Rio de la Plata. After the May Revolution of 1810 the United Provinces declared independence in 1816, and Jose de San Martin famously crossed the Andes to help liberate Chile and Peru. Waves of Italian and Spanish immigrants reshaped the country, which later endured military juntas and the 1982 Falklands War before returning to democracy in 1983.
ARG.funFact: Argentina is home to Aconcagua, the tallest mountain outside Asia at nearly 7,000 meters.

famous: constant trade winds for sailing and diving
ABW.culture: Arubans speak Papiamento alongside Dutch and English, celebrate one of the Caribbean's longest carnival seasons, and love keshi yena, a stuffed cheese casserole, with seafood.
ABW.history: Aruba was inhabited by the Caquetio, an Arawak people, when Spanish explorer Alonso de Ojeda claimed it in 1499, and the Dutch took control around 1636, running it for centuries as part of the Netherlands Antilles. In 1986 Aruba gained Status Aparte, becoming a separate autonomous country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. An oil refinery and then world-class tourism turned the dry, windy island into one of the Caribbean's wealthiest spots.
ABW.funFact: Aruba sits outside the Caribbean hurricane belt, so it enjoys sunny, dry weather almost all year.

BHS.culture: Bahamians celebrate Junkanoo with goatskin drums and elaborate costumes, eat cracked conch and peas n rice, and live between busy Nassau and quiet family islands.
BHS.history: The Lucayan Taino people lived there until Spanish slavers all but wiped them out soon after Columbus landed on San Salvador in 1492. Britain made the islands a colony in 1718 when Woodes Rogers drove out pirates like Blackbeard, and Loyalists with their enslaved workers arrived after the American Revolution. The Bahamas gained internal self-rule in 1964 and full independence in 1973, building a modern economy on tourism and banking.
BHS.funFact: Exuma's wild pigs paddle out to greet boats, and nobody knows exactly how they got there.

BRB.culture: Barbadians, called Bajans, love cricket, rum shops, fried flying fish with cou-cou, and the energetic Crop Over harvest festival each summer.
BRB.history: Home to Arawak and Carib peoples before the English settled it in 1627, Barbados became the world's first great sugarcane economy, worked by enslaved Africans whose descendants make up most of the population today. The island stayed British for over 300 years and peacefully gained independence in 1966. In November 2021 Barbados became a republic, replacing the British monarch with a president while keeping its Commonwealth ties.
BRB.funFact: Pop superstar Rihanna was born in Barbados and was named a National Hero when it became a republic.

BLZ.culture: Belize is a Caribbean-flavored corner of Central America where people speak English and Belizean Kriol, eat rice and beans with stewed chicken, and dance to punta music.
BLZ.history: Belize was the heart of the ancient Maya world, with great cities like Caracol and Xunantunich, and Spain claimed the region but never strongly settled it. English buccaneers and loggers instead cut mahogany and logwood here, and the territory became the colony of British Honduras before taking the name Belize and winning independence in 1981. Its mix of Maya, Mestizo, Creole, Garifuna and Mennonite communities makes it one of the most diverse countries in the Americas.
BLZ.funFact: The Great Blue Hole is a giant underwater sinkhole over 300 meters wide, made famous by diver Jacques Cousteau.

BMU.culture: Bermudians wear formal Bermuda shorts with knee socks and ties, celebrate the Gombey dancers at Christmas, and blend British tradition with island life.
BMU.history: Bermuda was accidentally discovered when the Sea Venture, carrying Sir George Somers, wrecked on its reefs in 1609, inspiring Shakespeare's The Tempest, and it was soon settled by the Virginia Company. It became Britain's oldest remaining overseas territory, serving for centuries as a strategic naval base. Today it is one of the world's leading insurance and finance centers with a famous golf-and-beaches tourism industry.
BMU.funFact: The Bermuda Triangle is an imaginary area where ships and planes have vanished, and scientists blame weather and human error rather than anything mysterious.

famous: cholitas in bowler hats and woven textiles
BOL.culture: Bolivians honor Pachamama, the earth mother, sip coca tea against the high altitude, eat saltenas, and fill the streets of La Paz and Oruro with carnival parades and folk dances.
BOL.history: Bolivia was home to the ancient Tiwanaku civilization and then the southern heartland of the Inca empire before Spain conquered it in the 1530s and called it Upper Peru, with the silver mountain of Potosi bankrolling the Spanish empire. Simon Bolivar and Antonio Jose de Sucre helped it win independence in 1825, and the country was named in Bolivar's honor. In 2006 Evo Morales became its first indigenous president, a landmark for a nation where most people have indigenous roots.
BOL.funFact: Salar de Uyuni is the largest salt flat on Earth, so flat and vast that satellites use it to calibrate their cameras.

BRA.culture: Brazilians dance samba through Carnival streets, cheer football like a religion, share feijoada and churrasco, and end the day with a caipirinha.
BRA.history: Brazil was home to millions of indigenous people organized in many river and forest cultures when Portuguese captain Pedro Alvares Cabral landed in 1500, making it the only Portuguese-speaking country in the Americas. It became a vast sugar, gold and coffee colony built on enslaved African labor, and in 1808 the Portuguese court itself fled Napoleon and moved to Rio de Janeiro, an event unique in colonial history. Brazil declared independence peacefully in 1822 under Emperor Pedro I, abolished slavery in 1888 and became a republic in 1889, growing into South America's giant.
BRA.funFact: Brazil is home to the largest Japanese community outside Japan, centered in Sao Paulo.

VGB.culture: The British Virgin Islands are a sailor's paradise where islanders race boats at summer regattas, eat fish and fungi, a cornmeal dish, and welcome visitors who island-hop by boat.
VGB.history: The islands were home to Arawak and Carib peoples before the Dutch settled them and England took over in 1672, building small plantations worked by enslaved Africans and collecting pirate legends around Tortola and Norman Island. They remained a quiet British colony, becoming part of a self-governing British overseas territory with tourism and offshore finance as their pillars.
VGB.funFact: Norman Island is said to have inspired Robert Louis Stevenson's Treasure Island.

CAN.culture: Canadians love hockey, poutine and Tim Hortons coffee, celebrate both English and French heritage, and fill Montreal and Toronto with summer festivals.
CAN.history: First Nations peoples and the Inuit have lived in Canada for thousands of years, and French explorers Jacques Cartier and Samuel de Champlain claimed and settled it, founding Quebec City in 1608 around the fur trade. Britain took control after the Seven Years' War in 1763, and in 1867 the provinces confederated under leaders like John A. Macdonald, expanding westward along the new railroads. Canada gradually gained full independence from Britain and today is a bilingual, multicultural nation known for peacekeeping and vast wilderness.
CAN.funFact: Canada has more lakes than all the other countries of the world combined.

BES.culture: These Dutch Caribbean islands mix Dutch, African and Caribbean influences, with diving on Bonaire, climbing Saba's volcano, and festivals with barbecue and soca music.
BES.history: Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba were home to Arawak peoples and later fought over by Spain and the Netherlands, becoming Dutch salt and sugar colonies, with Sint Eustatius a booming free port during the American Revolution. They formed part of the Netherlands Antilles until 2010, when instead of becoming autonomous like Aruba and Curacao they chose to become special municipalities of the Netherlands itself, using the euro and flying the Dutch flag.
BES.funFact: Bonaire's surrounding waters have been a protected marine park since 1979, making it one of the world's top diving spots.

CYM.culture: Caymanians celebrate Pirates Week with mock invasions, enjoy turtle stew and conch dishes, and live on some of the Caribbean's safest and wealthiest islands.
CYM.history: Cayman was uninhabited when Columbus sighted it in 1503 and named it Las Tortugas for its sea turtles, later becoming a British dependency settled by turtle fishers, shipwrecked sailors and a few pirates. Governed first under Jamaica, it stayed a British overseas territory after Jamaica's independence in 1962 and built itself into a global finance center alongside tourism.
CYM.funFact: Cayman charges no direct taxes on income, which helped turn it into one of the world's biggest banking hubs.

CHL.culture: Chileans eat empanadas and completos, dance the cueca during September's Fiestas Patrias, and drink world-class wine from a country 4,000 kilometers long.
CHL.history: Chile was home to the Mapuche, who famously resisted both the Inca empire and the Spanish, and to northern peoples under Inca influence before Pedro de Valdivia conquered the central valley and founded Santiago in 1541. Chile declared independence from Spain in 1818 with help from Jose de San Martin and Bernardo O'Higgins, later expanding north at Bolivia and Peru's expense in the War of the Pacific. The 20th century brought the 1973 coup against Salvador Allende and General Pinochet's dictatorship before democracy returned, and today the country stretches from the driest desert on Earth to Patagonian ice fields.
CHL.funFact: Chile owns Easter Island, one of the most remote inhabited places on Earth, famous for its giant moai statues.

famous: Gabriel Garcia Marquez and magical realism
COL.culture: Colombians dance cumbia and vallenato, eat arepas and bandeja paisa, and celebrate everything from the Flower Fair in Medellin to salsa nights in Cali.
COL.history: Colombia was home to sophisticated cultures like the Muisca and Tairona, whose golden treasures fed the legend of El Dorado, before Spain conquered it in the 1500s and made it the heart of the Viceroyalty of New Granada. Simon Bolivar won the Battle of Boyaca in 1819 and made Bogota the capital of his republic of Gran Colombia, which later split into Venezuela, Ecuador and Colombia. The country survived decades of internal conflict to become a vibrant democracy and one of the world's great coffee and flower exporters.
COL.funFact: Colombia records more bird species than any other country on Earth.

CRI.culture: Costa Ricans, called Ticos, greet each other with pura vida, eat gallo pinto for breakfast, and spend weekends in national parks full of sloths, toucans and monkeys.
CRI.history: Costa Rica was a quiet backwater of the Spanish empire after conquest in the 1520s, growing slowly around small farms rather than huge plantations, which shaped its unusually egalitarian colonial society. It gained independence from Spain in 1821 as part of Central America and abolished its army in 1948 after a brief civil war. Since then it has built one of the world's most stable democracies and pioneered ecotourism.
CRI.funFact: Costa Rica generates almost all of its electricity from renewable sources like rivers, wind and volcanic heat.

CUB.culture: Cubans dance to son and salsa, play dominoes on sidewalks, eat ropa vieja and drink strong coffee while Havana's vintage cars roll past colonial squares.
CUB.history: Home to Taino people, Cuba was claimed by Spain after Columbus arrived in 1492 and became one of the world's richest sugar colonies, worked by enslaved Africans with Havana as the empire's key port. Independence wars led by Jose Marti drew in the United States, and Cuba became independent in 1902 under strong American influence. Fidel Castro's revolution of 1959 turned Cuba communist, leading to the 1962 Missile Crisis and a US embargo that still shapes daily life on the island.
CUB.funFact: Cuba banned Christmas for nearly 30 years until Pope John Paul II's 1998 visit helped bring the holiday back.

CUW.culture: Curacaoans speak Papiamento, dance through a long carnival season, and enjoy keshi yena and beach parties in Willemstad's colorful streets, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
CUW.history: Inhabited by Caquetio Arawaks, Curacao was claimed for Spain in 1499 and seized by the Dutch in 1634, becoming a hub of the Dutch West India Company and its Atlantic slave trade. It formed part of the Netherlands Antilles until 2010, when it became an autonomous country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands, running an economy of oil refining, tourism and finance.
CUW.funFact: The bitter laraha orange grown on Curacao gives Blue Curacao liqueur its color and name.

DMA.culture: Dominicans celebrate Carnival and Creole Day with patois songs, calypso and mountain-grown food, and proudly call their island Waitukubuli, meaning tall is her body.
DMA.history: Dominica was home to Arawak and then Kalinago (Carib) people, who resisted European settlement so fiercely that the island remained largely indigenous longer than almost any other Caribbean island, and a Kalinago Territory still exists on its east coast today. France and Britain fought over it repeatedly, with Britain ruling from the late 1700s until independence in 1978. Known as the Nature Island, Dominica protects its volcanic rainforest and has become a leader in Caribbean ecotourism.
DMA.funFact: Dominica's Boiling Lake is one of the largest boiling lakes in the world, a cauldron of gray steam in a volcanic crater.

DOM.culture: Dominicans live for winter league baseball, dance merengue and bachata at every gathering, and eat La Bandera, the daily plate of rice, beans and meat.
DOM.history: Santo Domingo, founded by Bartholomew Columbus in 1496, was the first permanent European city in the Americas and Spain's colonial capital, home to the region's first cathedral and university, while the island's Taino people were nearly destroyed by conquest and disease. Haiti occupied the whole island in 1822, and the Spanish-speaking east broke free in 1844 as the Dominican Republic. The 20th century brought dictatorship under Rafael Trujillo until 1961, and the country now thrives on tourism, agriculture and exporting baseball talent.
DOM.funFact: The Dominican Republic produces more major league baseball players per person than any other country.

famous: the Middle of the World monument
ECU.culture: Ecuadorians eat ceviche and llapingachos, celebrate Andean festivals like Inti Raymi, and shop Otavalo's famous market for colorful woven textiles.
ECU.history: Ecuador was the northern heart of the Inca empire, with Quito as a great capital, until Spanish forces under Sebastian de Benalcazar conquered it in the 1530s. Antonio Jose de Sucre won the Battle of Pichincha in 1822 to liberate it, and Ecuador joined Bolivar's Gran Colombia before becoming a separate republic in 1830. The country later lost about half its territory to Peru in the 1941 war, discovered oil in the Amazon and became famous for Darwin's 1835 visit to the Galapagos, which helped inspire his theory of evolution.
ECU.funFact: The famous Panama hat actually comes from Ecuador, named for the canal workers who wore it.

SLV.culture: Salvadorans eat pupusas with pickled curtido, celebrate the Fiestas Agostinas, and live between coffee farms, volcano ridges and surf towns.
SLV.history: El Salvador was home to Maya cities and then the Pipil people, whose way of life is preserved at sites like Tazumal and the buried village of Joya de Ceren, before Pedro de Alvarado conquered it for Spain in the 1520s. It joined Central America's independence from Spain in 1821 and later became a separate republic as the federation broke up. Coffee wealth concentrated in few hands fueled a brutal civil war from 1979 to 1992, remembered for Archbishop Oscar Romero's assassination, and the country has since rebuilt with a huge diaspora and a recent boom in tourism and Bitcoin adoption.
SLV.funFact: In 2021 El Salvador became the first country in the world to make Bitcoin legal currency.

FLK.culture: The few thousand islanders, nicknamed Kelpers, live a quiet British life of wool, tea and pubs in Stanley, with wildlife watching as the main attraction.
FLK.history: Britain claimed the Falklands in 1765, and Argentina has claimed them ever since as the Islas Malvinas, inherited from Spanish colonial claims. In 1982 Argentina's military junta invaded, but Britain under Margaret Thatcher sent a naval task force that retook the islands after a short war. A 2013 referendum saw islanders vote overwhelmingly to stay British, and the territory now lives from sheep, fishing and tourism.
FLK.funFact: There are over half a million sheep in the Falklands but only around 3,500 people.

famous: the penal colony of Devil's Island
GUF.culture: French Guiana blends Creole, Maroon, Hmong and European communities, with street markets, a big carnival, and dishes of rice, fish and peppers.
GUF.history: Home to indigenous peoples and to Maroons descended from escaped African slaves, French Guiana was colonized by France in the 1600s and became a notorious penal colony from 1852 to 1953, with Devil's Island holding prisoners like Alfred Dreyfus. Today it is an official French overseas department, using the euro and electing deputies to Paris. Its economy and identity are tied to the Guiana Space Centre at Kourou, which has launched Europe's rockets since 1968.
GUF.funFact: French Guiana is legally part of France, making it the largest piece of the European Union in the Americas.

GRL.culture: Greenlanders, mostly Inuit Kalaallit people, hunt and fish, celebrate national day every June, and live in colorful coastal towns under the midnight sun.
GRL.history: Greenland was settled for thousands of years by Paleo-Eskimo peoples, then briefly by Norse colonists led by Erik the Red around 985 AD, before the Thule Inuit, ancestors of today's Greenlanders, arrived. Denmark claimed the island in 1721 through missionary Hans Egede and still rules it as an autonomous territory, with home rule since 1979. Wartime and Cold War bases like Thule, and today's melting ice cap, keep Greenland in world headlines as it moves toward possible full independence.
GRL.funFact: Greenland is the world's largest island, and about 80 percent of it lies under ice.

GRD.culture: Grenadians celebrate Spice Mas carnival with jab jab devil dancers, eat oil down, a one-pot breadfruit stew, and farm cocoa, nutmeg and spices on steep green hills.
GRD.history: Home to Arawak and Carib peoples, Grenada was sighted by Columbus in 1498, colonized by the French in 1650 after fierce Carib resistance and taken by the British in 1763, both building sugar and spice plantations on enslaved labor. It gained independence in 1974 and was shaken by a 1983 coup and a US-led invasion before returning to parliamentary democracy. Its nutmeg and cocoa keep it known as the Spice Isle.
GRD.funFact: Grenada is one of the world's top nutmeg producers, and its national flag even shows a nutmeg.

famous: Creole cuisine like accras and colombo
GLP.culture: Guadeloupe's Creole culture blends French and African roots, with spice-scented markets, zouk music, and carnival parades in every town.
GLP.history: Guadeloupe was home to Arawak and Carib peoples before France claimed it in 1635 and built one of the world's richest sugar colonies on enslaved African labor. Slavery was abolished in 1848, when Victor Schoelcher signed France's abolition decree, and the island became an official French department in 1946. Today Guadeloupe is part of France itself, using the euro and sending representatives to the National Assembly in Paris.
GLP.funFact: Guadeloupe is shaped like a butterfly, with two main islands joined by bridges across a narrow saltwater channel.

GTM.culture: Guatemalans, many of Maya heritage, weave brilliant huipil shirts, eat pepian and tortillas, and carpet Antigua's streets with sawdust art during Semana Santa.
GTM.history: Guatemala was the heart of the classic Maya civilization, with towering cities like Tikal and the even older El Mirador, until Pedro de Alvarado conquered it for Spain in the 1520s and crushed the K'iche' kingdom. It became the seat of the Captaincy General of Guatemala, gained independence from Spain in 1821 and later anchored the short-lived Central American federation. A long civil war from 1960 to 1996 scarred the country, but Maya culture remains a living force in highland villages today.
GTM.funFact: Tikal's temple pyramids appear in the first Star Wars movie, doubling as scenery on the rebel base moon Yavin 4.

GUY.culture: Guyana blends Afro-Guyanese, Indo-Guyanese and indigenous communities, sharing curries and roti, rum shops, cricket and the Mashramani republic festival.
GUY.history: Guyana was settled by the Dutch in the 1600s as the colonies of Essequibo and Berbice, passed to Britain in 1814 and grew sugar plantations that first used enslaved Africans and later brought indentured workers from India. It gained independence in 1966 under Forbes Burnham and became a republic in 1970, the only English-speaking country in South America. Recent offshore oil discoveries have turned it into one of the world's fastest-growing economies.
GUY.funFact: Kaieteur Falls drops 226 meters in a single plunge, roughly five times the height of Niagara Falls.

HTI.culture: Haitians dance kompa and rara, practice Vodou alongside Christianity, eat griot and rice and beans, and fill streets with vivid painting and craft.
HTI.history: Haiti was home to Taino people before France turned its colony of Saint-Domingue into the richest sugar colony on Earth, worked by hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans. Inspired by the French Revolution, the enslaved rose in 1791 under Toussaint Louverture and, after his capture, Jean-Jacques Dessalines defeated Napoleon's armies and declared independence on January 1, 1804, creating the world's first Black republic. The young nation was forced to pay France a crushing indemnity, and its later story includes dictatorships under the Duvaliers and devastating earthquakes, yet its revolution remains one of history's boldest freedom stories.
HTI.funFact: Haiti in 1804 became the first country in history founded by a successful slave revolt and the first to permanently abolish slavery.

HND.culture: Hondurans fold fillings into baleadas, celebrate La Feria Juniana carnival in San Pedro Sula, and follow football matches with national passion.
HND.history: Honduras was home to great Maya cities like Copan, famous for its carved stelae, before Spain conquered it in the 1520s and mined it for silver. It gained independence from Spain in 1821, drifted in and out of the Central American federation and became the classic banana republic as American fruit companies dominated its economy in the 20th century. Recent decades brought political turmoil including the 2009 coup, but Honduras also grows world-renowned coffee and draws divers to its reefs.
HND.funFact: Honduras's Bay Islands sit beside the Mesoamerican Reef, the second largest coral reef system in the world.

JAM.culture: Jamaicans speak Patois, eat jerk chicken and ackee with saltfish, play cricket and football, and move to reggae and dancehall everywhere they go.
JAM.history: Jamaica's Taino people were nearly wiped out after Columbus landed in 1494 and Spain claimed the island, and in 1655 England captured it, turning it into a sugar colony worked by enslaved Africans and a haven for pirates like Henry Morgan. Slavery ended in 1834 and Jamaica became independent from Britain in 1962. The island then gave the world reggae, Rastafari and Bob Marley, plus a sprint dynasty led by Usain Bolt.
JAM.funFact: Jamaica's unlikely 1988 bobsled team inspired the movie Cool Runnings.

MTQ.culture: Martinicans live a French-Creole life of markets, accras and boudin creole, carnival parades and beaches framed by tropical green hills.
MTQ.history: Inhabited by Carib peoples, Martinique was claimed for France in 1635 by Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc and became one of the world's wealthiest sugar colonies, built on enslaved African labor abolished in 1848. In 1902 Mount Pelee erupted and destroyed the city of Saint-Pierre, killing about 30,000 people in minutes. Martinique became a French department in 1946 and is the birthplace of both Empress Josephine, Napoleon's wife, and poet-politician Aime Cesaire, father of the negritude movement.
MTQ.funFact: Martinique is nicknamed the island of flowers and grows the sugarcane behind its famous agricole rum.

MEX.culture: Mexicans fill plazas with mariachi music, honor ancestors on Dia de los Muertos, eat tacos, tamales and mole, and cheer football matches and lucha libre wrestling.
MEX.history: Mexico is heir to great civilizations including the Olmec, Teotihuacan, the Maya and the Aztec empire, whose island capital Tenochtitlan amazed Hernan Cortes when the Spanish conquistador toppled it in 1521. New Spain grew rich on silver for 300 years until Father Miguel Hidalgo's cry for independence in 1810 led, by 1821, to an independent Mexico. The country lost half its territory to the United States in 1848, repelled a French invasion after the famous victory at Puebla in 1862 and remade itself in the Revolution of 1910, emerging as the large, proud and diverse nation of today.
MEX.funFact: Mexico gave the world chocolate, chili and corn, and Mexico City is slowly sinking into the old lake bed of Tenochtitlan.

MSR.culture: Montserratians celebrate St. Patrick's Day with a whole week of festivities, blend Irish and Creole traditions, and hike the green north of their volcanic island.
MSR.history: Settled by British and Irish colonists in 1632, Montserrat became known as the Emerald Isle of the Caribbean for its Irish planters and enslaved African workers. In 1995 the Soufriere Hills volcano erupted, burying the capital Plymouth in ash and forcing most of the population to leave, leaving it the only ghost capital in the Americas. The south remains an exclusion zone while the rebuilt north carries on the island's music legacy, including the recording studio where Beatles producer George Martin once drew rock stars.
MSR.funFact: Montserrat is the only place outside Ireland where St. Patrick's Day is a public holiday.

famous: Lake Nicaragua and volcano island Ometepe
NIC.culture: Nicaraguans perform the satirical Gueguense folk theater, eat gallo pinto twice a day, and dance through fiestas patronales in their colonial cities.
NIC.history: Nicaragua was home to thriving indigenous chiefdoms when Spanish conquistadors arrived, and Francisco Hernandez de Cordoba founded the rival cities of Granada and Leon in 1524, whose rivalry still marks national politics. It gained independence from Spain in 1821, later saw US Marines intervene and back the Somoza family dictatorship, until the Sandinista revolution ousted Anastasio Somoza in 1979. A devastating 1972 earthquake, civil war in the 1980s and elections since 1990 shaped the country that faces visitors today.
NIC.funFact: Lake Nicaragua is famous for being a freshwater lake with bull sharks, which leap rapids up the San Juan River from the sea.

PAN.culture: Panamanians celebrate carnival with water fights, eat sancocho and ceviche, and dress in the elaborate pollera, while Guna artisans sew colorful mola blouses.
PAN.history: Panama was home to several indigenous peoples when Vasco Nunez de Balboa crossed the isthmus in 1513 and became the first European to see the Pacific from the Americas. Spain used the isthmus as its treasure route, and Panama joined Colombia until 1903, when the United States backed an independence movement in order to build the Panama Canal, which opened in 1914. Panama regained full control of the canal on December 31, 1999, and today it is a world crossroads of shipping and finance.
PAN.funFact: In places in Panama you can watch the sun rise over the Pacific and set over the Atlantic, because the isthmus curves the opposite way from most coasts.

PRY.culture: Paraguayans sip cold terere all day from a shared gourd, speak both Spanish and Guarani, and eat sopa paraguaya and chipa cheese bread.
PRY.history: Home to Guarani peoples, Paraguay was claimed by Spain in the 1500s and became famous for Jesuit missions that sheltered indigenous communities from colonial abuse. It won independence from Spain in 1811 under the austere dictator Jose Gaspar Rodriguez de Francia, then suffered the catastrophic War of the Triple Alliance from 1864 to 1870 against Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay, losing most of its male population. Paraguay rebuilt around farming and giant dams, keeping Guarani culture at its heart.
PRY.funFact: Paraguay is the only country in the Americas where a majority of people speak an indigenous language, Guarani, alongside Spanish.

famous: Machu Picchu and the Inca Trail
PER.culture: Peruvians eat ceviche and pachamanca, grow thousands of potato varieties, dance huayno and marinera, and honor both the sun and Pachamama, the earth mother.
PER.history: Peru was the heart of the Inca empire, the largest state in the pre-Columbian Americas, centered on Cusco, until Francisco Pizarro conquered it in 1532 by capturing Emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca. Spanish Lima became a colonial capital while Andean silver fed the Spanish crown through forced indigenous labor. Peru declared independence in 1821 with Jose de San Martin and sealed it in 1824 when Simon Bolivar and Antonio Jose de Sucre won the battles of Junin and Ayacucho, and today its Inca ruins and cuisine draw visitors from everywhere.
PER.funFact: Peru grows more than 3,000 varieties of potato, and the Nazca Lines can only be fully seen from the air.

famous: the forts of Old San Juan
PRI.culture: Puerto Ricans, called Boricua, dance salsa and reggaeton, eat mofongo and roast lechon, and pack Old San Juan each January for the SanSe street festival.
PRI.history: Home to Taino people, Puerto Rico was claimed by Spain after Columbus's second voyage in 1493 and became a fortress colony guarding the Caribbean, with San Juan's massive El Morro castle rising in the 1500s. Spain ceded the island to the United States in 1898 after the Spanish-American War, and Puerto Ricans became US citizens in 1917. Today it is an unincorporated US territory that debates its political future while exporting music, baseball stars and culture worldwide.
PRI.funFact: Mosquito Bay on the island of Vieques holds the Guinness record as the world's brightest bioluminescent bay, glowing blue at night.

BLM.culture: St. Barts is a chic French island where celebrities, sailors and locals share croissants, Creole-accented French and small beach restaurants.
BLM.history: St. Barthelemy was claimed by France in 1648 and given to Sweden in 1784, when King Gustav III turned its capital into the free port of Gustavia, before France bought it back in 1878. Colonization never thrived on the dry, small island, so it escaped the big plantation economy. Today it is a French overseas collectivity and one of the world's most glamorous vacation spots.
BLM.funFact: The capital Gustavia still bears the name of Sweden's King Gustav III, a leftover of the island's Swedish years.

KNA.culture: Kittitians and Nevisians celebrate Carnival and Culturama, eat goat water stew and johnnycakes, and spend Sundays on cricket grounds and beach bars.
KNA.history: St. Kitts was the first permanent British colony in the Caribbean, settled in 1623 by Sir Thomas Warner, and the twin islands became the sugar heart of the empire, guarded by Brimstone Hill fortress, called the Gibraltar of the West Indies. Nevis was the birthplace of American founding father Alexander Hamilton and the wedding place of Admiral Nelson. The two islands became independent from Britain together in 1983, the newest Caribbean nation at the time.
KNA.funFact: St. Kitts has the Caribbean's last working railway, once used to haul sugarcane and now a scenic tourist train.

LCA.culture: St. Lucians speak English and Kweyol, compete between the La Rose and La Marguerite flower societies, and eat green figs and saltfish.
LCA.history: St. Lucia changed hands between France and Britain 14 times, more than any other Caribbean island, before Britain finally held it from 1814, leaving behind French Creole language and Catholic tradition. Its people blended African, French and British heritage into a distinct Kweyol culture. The island became independent in 1979 and honors two Nobel laureates, poet Derek Walcott and economist Arthur Lewis.
LCA.funFact: St. Lucia has produced two Nobel Prize winners, arguably the most per capita of any country on Earth.

famous: some of the Caribbean's best dining
MAF.culture: The French side of St. Martin mixes Parisian cafes and Creole kitchens, with duty-free shopping in Marigot and beaches on every cove.
MAF.history: Sighted by Columbus in 1493, the small island was shared between France and the Netherlands in 1648, and legend says the border was drawn by a Frenchman walking north and a Dutchman walking south, leaving the French side bigger. Saint-Martin is today an overseas collectivity of France, while the southern half, Sint Maarten, belongs to the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Hurricane Irma devastated the island in 2017, and it has rebuilt around tourism.
MAF.funFact: Legend says the island's border was set by two walkers, one French and one Dutch, and France ended up with the larger share.

famous: baguettes and boulangeries in North America
SPM.culture: The roughly 6,000 islanders live a French coastal life of fishing, fresh bread, wine and hockey, just a boat ride from Newfoundland.
SPM.history: A French fishing outpost since the 1600s, Saint Pierre and Miquelon was contested by France and Britain for a century before France kept it in the treaties of 1763 and 1814. During American Prohibition the islands boomed as a smuggling depot for liquor headed to the United States. They remain France's last foothold in North America, a self-governing overseas collectivity using the euro.
SPM.funFact: Saint Pierre and Miquelon is the last piece of France in North America, sitting just 20 kilometers off the Canadian coast.

VCT.culture: Vincentians dance through Vincy Mas, eat roasted breadfruit with jackfish, and fish and sail among the 32 islands of their chain.
VCT.history: St. Vincent was home to the Kalinago and to the Black Caribs, descendants of shipwrecked Africans and Carib people, who resisted European control for nearly two centuries until Britain deported thousands after the Carib War of 1796. The island then grew sugar under British rule and gained independence in 1979, the same year its La Soufriere volcano erupted. Its southern Grenadines, including Bequia and Mustique, anchor one of the world's most famous sailing cultures.
VCT.funFact: St. Vincent's botanic garden, founded in 1765, is the oldest in the Western Hemisphere and received breadfruit trees brought by Captain Bligh.

SXM.culture: Sint Maarten's Dutch side loves beach bars, carnival in April and May, and a mix of languages and island foods from more than a hundred nationalities.
SXM.history: The Dutch took the island in the 1600s and split it with France in 1648, running salt ponds and sugar plantations with enslaved labor, and later sharing the growth of tourism across the island. Once part of the Netherlands Antilles, Sint Maarten became a separate constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in 2010. Hurricane Irma leveled much of it in 2017, but the island rebuilt around its famous beaches and Princess Juliana airport.
SXM.funFact: Maho Beach sits directly under an airport runway, so landing jets pass just meters over sunbathers' heads.

famous: rainforest covering most of the country
the wooden old town of Paramaribo
SUR.culture: Suriname is a melting pot of Creole, Hindustani, Javanese, Maroon and indigenous peoples, sharing roti, pom and barbecues and celebrating each other's holidays.
SUR.history: Suriname was claimed by the English in the 1600s and traded to the Dutch in 1667 in exchange for New Amsterdam, today's New York City. Its plantations, worked by enslaved Africans, were notoriously brutal, and many escapees founded independent Maroon communities deep in the rainforest, later joined by indentured workers from India and Java. Suriname became independent from the Netherlands in 1975 and remains the only Dutch-speaking country in South America.
SUR.funFact: The Dutch traded New York for Suriname in 1667, and Suriname still speaks Dutch to this day.

TTO.culture: Trinidadians and Tobagonians party through Carnival in dazzling costumes, eat doubles and roti, and play pan in steel bands that echo around the world.
TTO.history: Home to indigenous peoples, Trinidad was claimed by Spain in 1498 and left quiet until French planters and enslaved Africans arrived in the late 1700s, after which Britain captured it in 1797. Workers from India came after slavery ended, creating today's rich African and Indian cultural mix. Trinidad and Tobago became independent in 1962 and gave the world Carnival, calypso, soca and the steel pan, often called the only major acoustic instrument invented in the 20th century.
TTO.funFact: Trinidad's Pitch Lake is the world's largest natural deposit of asphalt, and it once paved streets in New York and London.

TCA.culture: Islanders, called Belongers, celebrate with music and masquerade, eat conch fritters and fresh fish, and live a relaxed British-Caribbean life.
TCA.history: The Turks and Caicos were home to Taino peoples and later became a salt-collecting outpost for Bermudian settlers from the 1600s, with reefs that wrecked ships and hid pirates. They were governed alongside Jamaica until Jamaica's independence in 1962, when they became a separate British overseas territory. Today tourism, offshore finance and some of the world's best beaches drive the islands.
TCA.funFact: The islands are named after the Turk's cap cactus, whose red top reminded settlers of a Turkish fez.

USA.culture: Americans celebrate Thanksgiving and the Fourth of July, love road trips, burgers and apple pie, and export music, movies and sports around the world.
USA.history: The land was home to hundreds of indigenous nations, from the Ancestral Puebloans to the Cherokee and Sioux, before Spanish, French, Dutch and English colonization, with the English founding Jamestown in 1607 and Plymouth in 1620. Thirteen colonies declared independence in 1776, won the Revolutionary War under George Washington and wrote the Constitution in 1787. The nation expanded westward, fought a Civil War over slavery that ended in 1865, absorbed waves of immigrants and rose through two world wars to become the world's largest economy.
USA.funFact: In 1867 the United States bought Alaska from Russia for about two cents an acre, a deal mockingly called Seward's Folly.

VIR.culture: Virgin Islanders celebrate a carnival on each island, eat pate and johnnycake, and blend West African and Danish heritage with everyday American life.
VIR.history: The islands were home to Taino and Carib peoples and later became a Danish colony from the 1660s, running sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans amid the era's pirate legends. Denmark sold the islands to the United States in 1917 for 25 million dollars, partly to guard the Panama Canal during World War I. Today they are a US territory where residents are American citizens living on Caribbean time.
VIR.funFact: The US Virgin Islands drive on the left, a holdover from the Danish era, even though they use American cars and dollars.

URY.culture: Uruguayans carry a thermos and mate gourd everywhere, grill world-famous beef, and celebrate the world's longest carnival season with murga songs and candombe drums.
URY.history: Home to Charua peoples, Uruguay was contested between Spain and Portugal, with Spain founding Montevideo in 1726 as a fortress against Portuguese Brazil. Jose Gervasio Artigas led the independence struggle, and in 1828 Britain brokered a deal that created Uruguay as a buffer state between Argentina and Brazil. The country hosted and won the first FIFA World Cup in 1930 and is today one of South America's most stable and progressive democracies.
URY.funFact: Uruguay hosted and won the first FIFA World Cup in 1930, beating Argentina 4-2 in the final.

VEN.culture: Venezuelans stuff arepas with everything, dance salsa and merengue, celebrate carnival in costume and follow major league baseball like a religion.
VEN.history: Home to indigenous peoples, Venezuela was colonized by Spain in the 1500s and got its name, meaning little Venice, from stilt houses explorers saw on Lake Maracaibo, growing rich on cacao and later oil. Caracas-born Simon Bolivar led the independence struggle, declared in 1811 and secured with the 1821 victory at Carabobo, and Venezuela became a founding part of Bolivar's Gran Colombia. The modern era brought oil booms, the 1999 election of Hugo Chavez and deep political and economic change.
VEN.funFact: Angel Falls is the world's tallest waterfall, plunging 979 meters off a flat-topped mountain called a tepui.
